case_info.scenario: A 3-month-old male infant presented with a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in their right orbital and temporal region over 2 months. Examination revealed a firm, nontender, 5 × 4-cm mass with proptosis. The overlying skin exhibited a slight bluish discoloration. Computed tomography (CT) showed a large lytic lesion with a soft tissue component and spiculated, aggressive type of periosteal reaction with mild hyperostosis of the underlying bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a precontrast T1 hyperintense lesion with few hypointense areas, T2 hypointense spiculations and intense postcontrast enhancement and mild diffusion restriction (Figure 1). Chest and abdominal screening using low-dose CT showed no distant disease. The tumor was excised with clear margins, and histopathology showed a biphasic pattern of small neuroblastlike cells and larger melanin-containing epithelial cells. No evidence of locoregional or distant recurrence was observed after 1 year of follow-up.
case_info.caption: A, Axial computed tomography (CT) in bone window showing spiculated periosteal reaction (arrowhead) within the right frontal bone with associated soft tissue component. B, Corresponding axial T2-weighted magnetic resonance image (MRI) showing a predominantly T2 hypointense soft tissue mass in the right orbitofrontal region.
case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

dialogue_history.text: After excision, the primary management for melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy is typically observation, as these tumors often have a good prognosis and low recurrence rates. Regular follow-ups are essential, generally every 3 to 6 months for the first couple of years, monitoring for any signs of recurrence through physical examinations and imaging if indicated. In rare cases where there is a high risk of recurrence or if the tumor is incompletely excised, additional treatments like chemotherapy may be considered, but that's not common. Overall, the focus remains on vigilant follow-up and reassurance to the family.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

A 3-month-old male infant presented with a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in their right orbital and temporal region over 2 months. 1. Mental Demand

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

case_info.scenario: A 3-month-old male infant presented with a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in their right orbital and temporal region over 2 months. Examination revealed a firm, nontender, 5 × 4-cm mass with proptosis. The overlying skin exhibited a slight bluish discoloration. Computed tomography (CT) showed a large lytic lesion with a soft tissue component and spiculated, aggressive type of periosteal reaction with mild hyperostosis of the underlying bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a precontrast T1 hyperintense lesion with few hypointense areas, T2 hypointense spiculations and intense postcontrast enhancement and mild diffusion restriction (Figure 1). Chest and abdominal screening using low-dose CT showed no distant disease. The tumor was excised with clear margins, and histopathology showed a biphasic pattern of small neuroblastlike cells and larger melanin-containing epithelial cells. No evidence of locoregional or distant recurrence was observed after 1 year of follow-up.

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5
